candidate.title: Constraint-Aware Computational Generation of Loom-Compatible Asante Kente Patterns
candidate.workingTitle: Constraint-Aware Computational Generation of Loom-Compatible Asante Kente Patterns
candidate.summary: Can AI reliably generate patterns to weave? The refined direction is computational generation of structurally valid selected Asante Kente patterns and instructions for a specified Bonwire narrow-strip loom context.
candidate.shortDescription: A Ghana-grounded computational-design study of selected Asante Kente structures, constraint-aware generation, and loom-compatible instructions.
candidate.ghanaianRelevance: Directly grounded in Ghanaian textile practice. The scope must stay on selected structures rather than all Kente traditions.
candidate.technicalContribution: A layered computational representation linking visible design, weave structure, and Bonwire narrow-strip-loom execution; explicit constraints for a bounded pattern class; and a generation/validation method. The traditional narrow-strip loom and any broadloom translation must be treated as distinct contexts.

feasibility.rationale: This is a planning assessment. Feasibility depends on reliable weave-structure information and a testable definition of loom compatibility.

candidate.dataRequirements: Documented examples of selected Asante Kente structures, motif-to-draft mappings, point-paper grids, and loom-specific information for the Bonwire narrow-strip loom. Badoe (2005) and Badoe & Opoku-Asare are priority documentation leads but require full-text/bibliographic verification. Practitioner validation is desirable and must be confirmed early.
candidate.evaluationDesign: Compare unconstrained generation with constraint-aware generation using machine-checkable structural validity, constraint satisfaction, diversity, and completeness/consistency of weaving instructions. If practitioner access is secured, add expert assessment and possibly physical validation. Image similarity or visual plausibility alone cannot establish weaveability.
majorRisks: The loom type, bounded pattern class, and formal definition of compatibility are not yet fixed.
A visually plausible image may not encode the interlacing or execution sequence needed to weave it.
The 2024–2026 textile-generation and co-design leads have incomplete or unverified bibliographic details; they cannot yet establish novelty or a gap.
If practitioner or loom access is unavailable, claims must be limited to formal structural validity rather than production-ready execution.
openDecisions: Which specific Kente structures (e.g. bounded structures documented in the literature) will be included?
What exact Bonwire narrow-strip-loom parameters and execution instructions can be documented and validated?
Can the representation cover warp/weft and supplementary-weft structure, draft, heddling, shafts, and tie-up—or must it be restricted to a subset?
Can experienced Bonwire weavers validate the rules and a small number of generated instructions within the MPhil timeframe?
How should the thesis distinguish traditional narrow-strip-loom execution from broadloom translation?

nodes.title: Plausible textile images are not necessarily weavable structures
nodes.summary: A generated textile image can look convincing while failing to encode a valid weave structure or a sequence that a specified loom can execute.
nodes.detail: The initial idea was whether AI could reliably generate patterns that can be woven. The research was narrowed after considering recent textile-generation work: generic image generation is not a defensible novelty claim by itself. The computing problem is whether selected Asante Kente structures can be represented explicitly and generated subject to structural and loom-specific constraints. The thesis must define the pattern class and loom context rather than generalise to all Kente traditions. The November discussion narrowed the context toward executable instructions for a Bonwire narrow-strip loom. This must be distinguished from broadloom examples or translations; the traditional loom versus broadloom relationship remains an open technical and cultural boundary.
assumptions: A bounded set of structures is sufficient for an MPhil contribution.
A formal representation can capture the constraints needed for the chosen loom and pattern class.
Visual similarity is not evidence of weaveability.
risks: The research may become textile documentation rather than IT unless the representation, constraint model, generator, and evaluation are technically central.
Practitioner knowledge may be needed to validate the rules.

nodes.title: How can selected Asante Kente weaving structures be represented computationally and used to generate novel patterns that satisfy defined Bonwire narrow-strip-loom constraints?
nodes.summary: How can selected Asante Kente structures be encoded and generated as patterns and instructions that satisfy explicit constraints for a Bonwire narrow-strip loom?
nodes.detail: The central question is not whether an image model can draw Kente-like cloth. It is how selected Asante Kente structures can be encoded computationally, how constraints derived from the selected weaving context can be enforced, and how generated outputs can be evaluated for structural validity. The scope must be fixed to one bounded pattern class and one loom context. The working scope discussed is Bonwire narrow-strip-loom instructions. Broadloom examples in educational documentation should not be assumed to validate traditional narrow-strip execution.

nodes.title: Why this is a computing problem
nodes.summary: The contribution has to be a representation, a constraint model, and an evaluation, not only a description of Kente.
nodes.detail: This direction fits MPhil IT when its main contribution is a formal representation, a computational constraint model, a generation/repair method, and reproducible evaluation. The cultural context grounds the problem but is not a substitute for the computing contribution.

nodes.title: Grounded in Asante weaving practice
nodes.summary: Grounded in Asante weaving practice
nodes.detail: The direction is grounded in Ghanaian textile practice. That relevance does not by itself make the work a computing contribution, and it does not license claims about all Kente traditions.

nodes.title: A representation and a constraint check
nodes.summary: A representation and a constraint check
nodes.detail: The technical object can be modelled in layers: visible design/motif arrangement; underlying weave structure; loom-specific execution constraints; and validation of the mapping between them. A narrow-loom practice and broadloom translation must not be treated as interchangeable. Candidate representation elements discussed include warp/weft and supplementary-weft structure, point-paper grids, motif-to-draft mappings, drafts, heddling, shafts, and tie-up. The final representation should include only the elements that can be documented and validated.

nodes.title: What would count as a contribution
nodes.summary: What would count as a contribution
nodes.detail: A defensible contribution could comprise (1) a machine-readable representation for a bounded set of Kente structures, (2) explicit structural/loom constraints, (3) a generator that rejects or repairs invalid candidates, and (4) an evaluation protocol that distinguishes visual appearance from structural validity and execution feasibility.

nodes.title: Structured representation of selected motifs
nodes.summary: Structured representation of selected motifs
nodes.detail: A small, documented, machine-readable corpus of selected motifs and associated weave structures. It should record provenance and scope; it is not intended as a complete catalogue of Kente. The literature discussion specifically referenced Ahwepan, Topreko, Faprenu, and Asasia as named structures documented by Badoe & Opoku-Asare (2014); verify the source and the scope before selecting any of them.

nodes.title: Formal constraint model
nodes.summary: Formal constraint model
nodes.detail: A formal set of structural and loom-specific constraints that can be tested automatically. Each rule should be traceable to documentation or practitioner validation.

nodes.title: Generation method
nodes.summary: Generation method
nodes.detail: A computational method that generates candidate patterns under the selected representation and constraints, with explicit handling of invalid outputs (rejection, repair, or constrained search).

nodes.title: Machine-checkable validation
nodes.summary: Machine-checkable validation
nodes.detail: A reproducible validator reporting rule violations, constraint satisfaction, structural validity, diversity, and instruction completeness. The validator must not equate pixel similarity with successful weaving.

nodes.title: External check, only if feasible
nodes.summary: External check, only if feasible
nodes.detail: If access and time permit, experienced weavers assess whether the representation and instructions correspond to the selected practice; a small physical weave test is optional and must not be promised before access is confirmed.
risks: Do not make physical production validation a dependency unless loom and practitioner access are secured early.

nodes.title: Computational textile generation
nodes.summary: Computational textile generation
nodes.detail: Methods that generate textile patterns, including recent learning-based and grammar-based leads.

nodes.title: Generation methods may optimise appearance
nodes.summary: Generation methods may optimise appearance
nodes.detail: The project discussions identified FabricGen/WeavingLLM, shape-grammar work, and other computational textile systems as important prior-art leads. One discussion described FabricGen/WeavingLLM as involving 1,142 drafts. These details are discovery notes only: the exact bibliographic records, system capabilities, and whether they encode physical loom constraints must be checked in the full texts. Generic textile generation is therefore not a safe novelty claim.

nodes.title: Visual plausibility may be produced without a specific weaving process
nodes.summary: Visual plausibility may be produced without a specific weaving process
nodes.detail: A possible gap is the distance between generating a visually plausible textile design and representing constraints that make a pattern valid for a specified weaving process. The existence and extent of this gap are unconfirmed until FabricGen/WeavingLLM, shape-grammar work, and other relevant systems are inspected for their representations, constraints, and validation methods.
assumptions: The selected prior systems may optimise visual or design-level output without modelling the selected loom process; this must be checked, not assumed.
validationRequirements: Extract each system’s input/output representation, weaving assumptions, structural constraints, and validation procedure.
Compare the exact scope of the systems against the chosen Asante Kente structures and loom context.

nodes.title: Structural patterns are documented for design education
nodes.summary: Structural patterns are documented for design education
nodes.detail: The project discussions referenced Badoe (2005), Badoe and Opoku-Asare, and other Ghanaian textile/Kente documentation as cultural and structural background. The exact bibliographic records and the extent to which these sources formalise motifs, weave structures, or loom execution remain to be verified. The discussion identified Badoe & Opoku-Asare (2014) as describing Ahwepan, Topreko, Faprenu, Asasia, motif/point-paper grids, drafts, heddling, shafts, tie-up, and composition rules, including student motif-to-draft-to-broadloom examples. This is a project literature note and needs direct source verification.

nodes.title: General textile models may not capture Asante Kente conventions
nodes.summary: General textile models may not capture Asante Kente conventions
nodes.detail: A possible contribution is a machine-readable representation specific to a bounded set of Asante Kente structures, rather than applying a generic textile representation unchanged. This is a candidate gap, not an established absence: existing textile grammars, design tools, and Kente documentation must be compared first. The potential technical distinction is not merely digitising motifs: it is preserving the relationship between motif, weave draft, and the specific loom execution process.
risks: Do not model all Kente traditions. Select a bounded set of structures.
validationRequirements: Determine whether existing Kente documentation already provides a formal representation suitable for computation.
Distinguish motif semantics, visual layout, weave structure, and loom execution in the comparison.

nodes.detail: The project discussions highlighted that co-design work on Ikat reportedly involved interpretation or modification by weavers and physical validation. This suggests that a generated digital design should not be treated as validated solely because it looks plausible. The precise study findings and evaluation protocol remain unverified.

nodes.title: Evaluation may not measure structural validity or weave compatibility
nodes.summary: Evaluation may not measure structural validity or weave compatibility
nodes.detail: A possible methodological gap is that visual or user-preference evaluation may not measure structural validity, constraint satisfaction, or loom compatibility. This needs direct comparison of evaluation criteria in the relevant papers; the Ikat co-design lead is not proof that all existing systems omit such measures.
validationRequirements: Extract metrics and validation methods from each directly relevant system.

nodes.title: Tools and papers may stop at the drawing
nodes.summary: Tools and papers may stop at the drawing
nodes.detail: The discussions repeatedly distinguished a digital pattern image from a weaving specification. A file may describe appearance without providing the interlacement, thread sequence, lift plan, or other loom-specific information needed for execution. Whether existing tools stop at the drawing must be checked against their actual outputs.

nodes.title: A digital pattern may not be an executable weaving specification
nodes.summary: A digital pattern may not be an executable weaving specification
nodes.detail: The potential gap is a missing or incomplete mapping from a generated visual pattern to a valid, executable specification for one selected loom context. The thesis should not claim production readiness unless the output format and physical execution are validated.
risks: If loom specifications or knowledgeable reviewers are not available, narrow the claim to structurally constrained pattern generation.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project discussions identify Tang et al. (2026), described as FabricGen/WeavingLLM, as a recent computational textile-generation lead; one discussion noted 1,142 drafts.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The exact paper and the 1,142-draft detail are not verified here. It is not established whether the system models a specific physical weaving process or loom-level constraints.
evidenceLinks.notes: Treat as a high-priority full-text verification task, not as confirmed evidence for the gap.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes describe Wang et al. (2026) as shape-grammar work that might bear on pattern structure.
evidenceLinks.limitation: It is not yet known whether the work addresses textile structure.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Badoe (2005) is cited in the project notes as an analytical study of Asante Kente structural patterns.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The notes do not establish a machine-readable specification or a generation algorithm.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes identify Badoe & Opoku-Asare (2014) as documenting Asante Kente structures including Ahwepan, Topreko, Faprenu, and Asasia, with motif/point-paper and draft-related instructional material.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The full text and bibliographic record have not been checked here. Notes mention broadloom examples; they do not establish Bonwire narrow-strip-loom execution rules.
evidenceLinks.notes: Priority full-text review. Extract the structures, draft notation, heddling, shafts, tie-up, and any limits on translating instructional examples to a traditional narrow-strip loom.

evidenceLinks.claim: Sawyerr et al. (2026) is a lead on Ghanaian textile AI.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Relevance to weave structure, rather than visual generation, is unverified.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project discussions describe an Ikat co-design study in which digital designs reportedly required interpretation or modification by weavers and physical validation.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Exact title, study protocol, sample, and findings are unverified. The observation cannot be generalised to Kente or all textile-generation systems.
evidenceLinks.notes: Extract how designers/weavers evaluated digital outputs and whether physical weaving was actually performed.

evidenceLinks.claim: weaveDraft is recorded as a software tool that may expose weave information.
evidenceLinks.limitation: No research paper has been identified, and its loom assumptions are unknown.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.
